question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the best linear combination of the measured SNPs (i.e., the additive genetic variance explained by those SNPs). A polygenic score is also a linear combination of SNPs, but its weights are estimated from finite samples and are therefore subject to sampling error, shrinkage, and incomplete tagging. Consequently, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any realizable PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) except in the unattainable limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained data. The qualifier “necessarily” therefore holds under all practical conditions.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be attributed to all SNPs in aggregate, but a polygenic score is always derived from a finite discovery sample whose effect-size estimates contain sampling error and are typically shrunk (e.g., via LDpred, PRS-CS). Consequently, even the best possible PGS captures only a noisy, incomplete subset of that total genetic signal, so its out-of-sample R² is necessarily lower than the SNP-heritability benchmark.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The polygenic score is constructed from finite-sample effect-size estimates that necessarily contain noise and shrinkage (even with methods like LDpred or PRS-CS), so the out-of-sample variance explained is bounded strictly below the SNP heritability that would be obtained from the true causal effects in the population. This gap persists regardless of sample size because new variants and interactions remain imperfectly tagged.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is additively tagged by the measured SNPs; it is therefore the theoretical upper bound on out-of-sample \(R^2\) that any linear predictor (i.e., any polygenic score) constructed from those SNPs can achieve. With infinite sample size and perfect estimation of effect sizes (or with methods such as LDpred-inf / SBayesR that recover the posterior mean under the correct infinitesimal model), the polygenic score’s \(R^2\) converges to \(h^2_{SNP}\). Hence the predictive ability is not *necessarily* strictly lower; it can equal the SNP heritability in the limit. In finite samples it is lower, but the statement claims necessity, which is false.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by all SNPs jointly (i.e., the theoretical upper bound attainable by any linear combination of those SNPs). A polygenic score is itself a finite linear combination of SNPs whose weights are estimated from finite data; therefore its out-of-sample \(R^2\) cannot exceed \(h^2_{SNP}\) and, under any realistic sample size, will be strictly smaller because of estimation error, imperfect linkage disequilibrium, and possible mismatches between discovery and target samples. Hence the predictive ability of a PGS is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The polygenic score is constructed from estimated effect sizes in a finite GWAS sample, which introduces shrinkage, imperfect tagging of causal variants, and winner's curse bias; as a result, the out-of-sample R² it achieves is bounded well below the SNP heritability that would be obtained from the full set of SNPs in an infinite sample. Even in the theoretical limit, practical construction of a PGS never recovers every last fraction of that SNP heritability.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by all SNPs in aggregate (typically estimated via methods like GREML or LD score regression). In contrast, a polygenic score is constructed from a finite set of effect-size estimates, usually pruned for independence and often limited to genome-wide significant loci or weighted by discovery-sample statistics that include noise. Because of imperfect tagging, winner's curse, population stratification residuals, and the fact that effect sizes are shrunk or thresholded, the out-of-sample variance captured by the score is a strict subset of the SNP-heritability signal. Hence the predictive R² is necessarily lower than h²_SNP.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-heritability of a phenotype is the theoretical upper bound on the out-of-sample variance that any additive polygenic score (PGS) constructed from the same set of SNPs can explain. Because effect-size estimates are necessarily imperfect (finite GWAS sample size, LD tagging error, winner’s curse, etc.), the realized R² of a PGS is strictly lower than this bound. Equality is only approached asymptotically with infinite data and perfect knowledge of every causal effect; in any real setting the inequality is strict.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that is (in principle) tagged by the SNPs in the population; it is an in-sample population parameter obtained under the assumption that the true effect sizes are known. A polygenic score, by contrast, is formed from effect-size estimates obtained in a finite discovery sample. Because those estimates contain sampling error, shrinkage, and possible model misspecification, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by the score is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) (except in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly representative data). Hence the predictive ability of any realizable polygenic score is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the optimal linear combination of all SNPs (i.e., the best linear predictor). A polygenic score constructed with the true (population) effect sizes for every SNP would therefore attain exactly this value; any empirical shortfall below \(h^2_{SNP}\) arises only from finite-sample estimation error, incomplete SNP coverage, or imperfect linkage disequilibrium, none of which are logically required by the definitions themselves. Hence the predictive \(R^2\) of a PGS is not necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by an optimal linear combination of all measured SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound attainable by any linear predictor built from those SNPs). A polygenic score is constructed from estimated rather than known effect sizes; finite GWAS sample sizes therefore introduce shrinkage/estimation error that necessarily attenuates the out-of-sample \(R^2\) below this bound. Even in the limit, practical PGS implementations (LD pruning, p-value thresholding, or regularization) further ensure the realized predictive \(R^2\) remains strictly lower than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Hence the statement holds.

11.text:

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total additive variance tagged by the measured SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound on variance that could be captured by an optimal linear combination of those SNPs). A polygenic score, however, is constructed from finite-sample effect-size estimates whose sampling error, winner’s-curse bias, imperfect LD tagging, and possible shrinkage or pruning steps all reduce the out-of-sample \(R^2\) below this bound. Consequently, the variance explained by any realizable PGS is necessarily strictly smaller than \(h^2_{SNP}\).

Final answer: True
